ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the attached figure there is a large equilateral-triangle grid, composed of many congruent small equilateral triangles; in the center there is a gray shaded polygon. Some of the boundary of the shaded region lies along grid lines, and some passes through small triangles, so area blocks of half a small triangle will appear. Reasoning: Take the area of one smallest equilateral triangle as 1 unit. Directly count the shaded part according to the horizontal grid bands in the figure from top to bottom, and count the half-triangles cut by the boundary in paired fashion: the shaded areas of each layer are respectively 0.5, 2.5, 4.5, 5.5, 5.5, 4 small-triangle units. The total is 0.5 + 2.5 + 4.5 + 5.5 + 5.5 + 4 = 22.5 small-triangle units. Each small equilateral triangle has area 4 cm², so the shaded area is 22.5 × 4 = 90 cm².

raw_record.question_text: In the diagram, the small equilateral triangles have area $4 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$. What is the area of the shaded region?

method.method_draft: Direct unit-triangle counting. First read the image as a large equilateral triangle subdivided into congruent smallest equilateral triangles, with a central shaded polygon whose sides cut through several of these small triangles. Use the grid lines already drawn in the picture to partition the shaded polygon into complete small equilateral triangles plus simple fractional pieces, mainly halves created where the straight shaded boundary cuts a small triangle. Pair complementary fractional pieces when possible, then total the shaded area in units of the smallest triangle. The count gives 22.5 small-triangle units. From the text, each small equilateral triangle has area 4 cm^2, so the shaded area is 22.5 × 4 = 90 cm^2.

method.method_draft: Coordinate/shoelace method. First read the image by identifying the vertices of the shaded polygon relative to the triangular lattice: the lower vertices lie on the base grid line, the left and right sides are vertical cuts through lattice points, and the top edge is a slanted segment whose endpoints are located by counting grid spacings. Let the side length of a smallest equilateral triangle be a and its altitude be h, so one small triangle has area ah/2 = 4. Assign Cartesian coordinates to the shaded polygon vertices in units of a horizontally and h vertically, as read from the diagram. Apply the shoelace formula, or equivalently decompose the polygon into trapezoids/triangles using these coordinates. The coordinate area simplifies to 22.5 times the area of one smallest triangle, hence 22.5 × 4 = 90 cm^2.
